title: Leading Team Members Who Dont Want a Relationship and Want to Be Left Alone to Do Their Work
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece confronts a modern tension: decades of leadership theory have pushed toward closer, more peer-like relationships between leaders and team members, yet a growing subset of workers -- often shaped by remote and digital-first norms -- actively reject that model and simply want to be left alone to do their work. The author frames this as more than a preference issue; accommodating it, they argue, undermines the trust and chemistry that let teams achieve things together. The recommended stance is firm: organizations should ask team members to adapt to organizational norms of engagement rather than restructuring norms around individual preferences for isolation, even while remaining willing to learn from other legitimate feedback.
points: A growing subset of team members, shaped by digital-first work culture, reject deeper relational engagement with leaders.
Accommodating full disengagement is framed as undermining the trust and chemistry that make collective results possible.
The piece distinguishes between learning from team members' input and tolerating rejection of core collaborative norms.
The recommended response is to require full engagement or, ultimately, to let resistant team members exit.
This tension is presented as a genuine test of contemporary, relationship-centered leadership philosophy.
quotes: In a challenge to the modern orthodoxy, some team members don’t want a relationship with their leader, preferring instead to do their work independently and remotely.
How does a leader engage team members who are good at what they do but disengage in an instant and have little desire to build a deeper connection to the leader, the organization, or its vision?
No team or organization can absorb beliefs and practices that are contrary to how it operates.
The best leaders ask team members to accommodate and adapt to the organization and not the other way around.
Those who insist on independence are welcome to take their skills elsewhere.
